paragraphs.text: On a hot summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. This effect, known as the urban heat island, was first described in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard, an amateur scientist who recorded temperatures in and around London over many years. He noticed that the difference was greatest not in the afternoon but at night.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The reasons are now well understood. Dark roads and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly after sunset. Tall buildings trap this warm air and block the wind that might otherwise carry it away. Cars, air-conditioning units and factories add further heat, and because cities have fewer trees and less open soil, there is less water evaporating to cool the air.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Higher temperatures are not simply uncomfortable. During heatwaves, the number of deaths in cities rises sharply, particularly among elderly people living alone. Warm nights are especially dangerous, because the body has no chance to recover from the heat of the day. Demand for electricity also increases as more people switch on air-conditioning, which in turn releases more heat into the streets.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Cities have tried a range of responses. Some paint roofs white or cover them with light-coloured materials that reflect sunlight. Others plant trees along streets, since a single mature tree can cool the air around it through shade and evaporation. In one European city, replacing a car park with a small park lowered the temperature of the surrounding streets by around two degrees on summer evenings.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: None of these measures is a complete solution. White roofs reduce the need for cooling in summer but can increase heating costs in winter in colder climates. Trees take many years to grow and need water, which may be scarce during the very heatwaves they are meant to relieve. Many planners now argue that the best results come from combining several small changes rather than relying on a single large project.
paragraphs.label: E
